title: CPU-side bottlenecks: tokenization, request parsing, threadpools, Python overhead
summary: Investigation into CPU-bound overheads observed in the serving runtime. Focus areas: tokenization cost per request, request parsing/validation pipeline, threadpool behavior, and Python interpreter/GIL overhead. Includes profiling methodology, microbenchmarks, flamegraph references, and mitigation recommendations.
content:
Background:
We’ve seen sustained elevated CPU utilization on host-level metrics while tail latency and cost-per-token remain suboptimal for short requests (prompt length < 128). This doc captures a focused investigation into the CPU-side work that lives outside the GPU/accelerator path: tokenization, request parsing & validation, threadpool behavior, and Python interpreter overhead (GIL, GC, call overhead).

Scope & goals:
- Measure per-request CPU cost for common short-request patterns (chat turn, single prompt)
- Attribute CPU time to tokenization, request parsing/validation, routing, and Python runtime overhead
- Identify high-impact mitigations that reduce p99 latency and per-request CPU time

Environment & test harness:
- Serving binary: redwood-served (local dev build, opt flags on)
- Test hardware: c6i.large-equivalent (8 vCPU) emulating control-plane processes; GPUs stubbed for CPU-only measurements
- Worker config: uvicorn + gunicorn with uvloop; default threadpool size 20 for blocking tasks
- Tokenizer: HuggingFace tokenizers via Python binding (Rust-backed) in most services; legacy codepaths fall back to pure-Python tokenizers for some routes
- Workload: synthetic HTTP POST to /v1/generate, 1k requests warmup, 10k sample requests at RPS=100 (poisson)

Methodology & tools:
- Sampling CPU profiler: py-spy (sampling, native stack traces) to get relative time spent in Python functions
- Native CPU perf: perf and perf-map-agent for C/C++ stacks
- Flamegraphs: speedscope JSON generated from py-spy and FlameGraph scripts
- Tracing: distributed tracing (jaeger) to correlate request-level timing to CPU samples
- Microbenchmarks: isolated tokenization loop (single-threaded & multithreaded), request parse/validate bench in-process, threadpool submit/execute latency test
- GC tracing: tracemalloc + gc.get_stats() during bench runs

High-level observations:
1) Tokenization cost:
   - For 32 token prompts, tokenization accounts for ~18-30% of CPU time on short requests on the observed codepath.
   - Rust-backed HF tokenizers are fast (~50-80 µs per short prompt), but we observed a legacy fallback (pure Python split/mapping code) on ~12% of production requests which costs ~600-900 µs.
   - Batch tokenization (tokenizing multiple prompts in one call) reduces per-prompt overhead by ~20-40% but requires request coalescing/queueing logic.

2) Request parsing & validation:
   - JSON parse + validation (pydantic) shows up as a significant contributor: ~200-500 µs per request depending on schema complexity.
   - Using orjson instead of Python stdlib json reduced parse time by ~2.5x in microbenchmarks.
   - Pydantic v1 validation cost is non-trivial when models are nested; switching to pydantic-core/pydantic v2 or hand-rolled light validation for hot paths reduced cost by ~300 µs.

3) Threadpool and concurrency behavior:
   - Threadpool submit/execute latency increases sharply under contention. With default threadpool max_workers=20 we saw queuing when RPS spikes, adding 100-200 µs of latency per submit.
   - Worker threads perform blocking tasks (filesystem reads for tokenization caches, small crypto ops for request signing, synchronous HTTP calls). Moving these to async or a dedicated pool reduced tail latency.
   - Oversubscription: CPU-bound Python + threadpool for blocking IO caused stalls due to GIL contention.

4) Python interpreter overhead (GIL/GC/call overhead):
   - py-spy indicates frequent short-lived Python frames (function entry/exit) that add up. Lower-level libraries (Rust-backed tokenizers) avoid this but many glue layers in our stack are Python.
   - GC: for these short-lived requests, GC non-generational tuning (or frequent minor collections) contributed ~3-8% CPU in some runs.

Representative numbers (short-request case, median over runs):
- Total CPU time per request (median): 2.1 ms
  - Tokenization: 0.5 ms (24%) [0.05-0.9ms depending on codepath]
  - JSON parse & validation: 0.35 ms (17%)
  - Routing / auth / TLS handling (user-space): 0.25 ms (12%)
  - Threadpool queue/submit overhead: 0.2 ms (10%)
  - Python interpreter overhead (frame overhead, GIL waits, GC): 0.35 ms (17%)
  - Other (misc): 0.45 ms (20%)

Flamegraph findings:
- Top hot spots are: fastapi.request._receive, pydantic.parse_obj, our legacy tokenization shim (tokenize_text_py), and concurrent.futures._base.ThreadPoolExecutor.submit.
- Native stacks show kernel scheduler wakeups when threadpool queuing spikes (indicating context switch costs).

Root causes & detailed notes:
- Mixed tokenizer usage: despite standardizing on HuggingFace tokenizers, a few legacy paths still call a pure-Python tokenizer when the model config lacks a tokenizer identifier. This creates a tail of slow requests.
- Heavy validation: user-supplied function-calling schemas (for tool-call routes) hit pydantic heavily. The validation graph contains nested lists/dicts leading to repeated type-checking.
- Threadpool usage pattern: request processing submits many small blocking tasks (cache lookup, small DB read) to the same threadpool used by the HTTP server. This creates imbalanced queuing and SLO increases under bursty traffic.
- Python glue overhead: multiple small Python-level wrappers around Rust/C libraries cause frequent interpreter transitions. While each transition is small, aggregated cost becomes material at RPS and for short-lived requests.

Mitigation recommendations (prioritized):
1) Eliminate legacy pure-Python tokenizer paths (high impact, low risk): audit model onboarding & default tokenizer lookup; enforce tokenizer presence in model metadata. Short-term: detect fallback at runtime and log+metrics; medium-term: fail fast or auto-attach HF tokenizers at model load.

2) Replace slow JSON/validation stack in hot paths (medium-high impact):
   - Use orjson for parsing and pydantic v2 / pydantic-core or msgpack for hot routes.
   - Alternatively, accept pre-parsed protobuf or compact binary payloads for internal service-to-service traffic.

3) Rework threadpool strategy (high impact):
   - Separate pools: a small bounded pool for CPU-bound tasks, a dedicated blocking-pool for IO/blocking tasks.
   - For HTTP worker processes, prefer async-first for non-CPU tasks; use run_in_executor with a dedicated executor for heavy blocking ops.
   - Tune max_workers based on CPU. Consider using a request-level semaphore to prevent unbounded enqueueing of blocking tasks.

4) Reduce Python interpreter overhead (medium impact):
   - Collapse hot wrapper layers: provide a single native extension that batches small ops (e.g., tokenization + mapping) to reduce round-trips.
   - Profile and inline critical hot functions in C/Rust (the tokenizers already help — expand similar approach to canonical caching layer).
   - Tune GC thresholds for the request pattern (fewer allocations; consider manual gc.disable()/enable() around hot loops if safe).

5) Tokenization caching & batching (medium-high impact, requires coord):
   - Add a small LRU of recent tokenization results keyed by raw prompt for repeated short prompts.
   - Opportunistic batching: coalesce tokenization for concurrent requests within a short window (e.g., 2-5ms) to amortize cost. Requires careful latency SLO experiments.

Quick wins implemented (experiments):
- Swapped stdlib json -> orjson on hot endpoints: median CPU/request dropped 0.15 ms, p99 improved ~7%.
- Detect-and-metric legacy tokenizer fallback: immediate visibility, flagged ~12% of traffic; plan to gate on model metadata.
- Introduced separate ThreadPoolExecutor for blocking IO in the HTTP path in a canary service: p99 reduced by ~12% under spike tests.

Open questions / tradeoffs:
- Batching tokenization introduces micro-delay (queueing) which may harm p50 for latency-sensitive customers. Need A/B test per route.
- Binary formats (protobuf/msgpack) reduce CPU but alter customer-facing API; internal services are good candidates.
- Rewriting wrappers in Rust/C++ has maintenance cost and release cadence impacts; prioritize for libraries with clear CPU ROI.

Next steps & ownership:
- Short-term (owner: Lena Morales): rollout orjson on all hot endpoints, add metrics for tokenizer fallback, increase logging for pydantic validation time (2 weeks).
- Mid-term (owner: Ravi Shah): implement dedicated blocking threadpool and semaphore gating in the HTTP worker process; run high-RPS spike tests and collect traces (4-6 weeks).
- Long-term (owner: Maya Chen): evaluate native extension that batches tokenization + canonical cache in Rust (quarterly project; requires spec & benchmarks).

Appendix: commands & microbench examples
- py-spy sampling: py-spy record -o profile.svg -- python -m served.main --config=local --workers=1 --bind=127.0.0.1:8080
- tokenization microbench: python -c "from tokenizers import Tokenizer; t=Tokenizer.from_file('tokenizer.json'); import time; s='hello world'*3; t0=time.time();[t.encode(s) for _ in range(10000)]; print((time.time()-t0)/10000)"
- request bench (wrk): wrk -t4 -c100 -d60s -s scripts/post_generate.lua http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/generate
- threadpool contention repro: small harness that submits 10k short blocking tasks to ThreadPoolExecutor with varying max_workers and measures queue latency.

Attachments & artifacts:
- flamegraphs (speedscope): link in linked_artifacts / confluence entry above
- microbenchmark data (csv): stored in internal S3: s3://redwood-dev/serving-runtime/profiles/2024-11-tokenization-bench.csv

Summary conclusion:
CPU-side work is a measurable and addressable contributor to per-request cost and tail latency, especially for short prompts. The largest near-term wins are removing legacy pure-Python tokenizers, moving JSON parsing/validation to faster serializers/validators, and separating blocking IO into dedicated pools. Medium-term work (native batching/caching and rewritten hot wrappers) will further reduce CPU time per request and improve cost efficiency.
